title: Tuesdays with Morrie: An Old Man, a Young Man, and Life's Greatest Lesson
author: Mitch Albom
target_audience: Adults seeking life lessons and personal growth
Readers interested in memoirs and real-life stories
Caregivers and those experiencing terminal illness
Anyone reflecting on life's meaning, relationships, and mortality
core_themes: The meaning of life and mortality
primary_purpose: To share the profound conversations and life lessons imparted by Morrie Schwartz, a terminally ill sociology professor, to his former student Mitch Albom, encouraging readers to reflect on what truly matters in life and to live with greater purpose, compassion, and understanding.

structure_format.narrative_style: Reflective, personal, and conversational, told in the first person
structure_format.organization: Structured around fourteen consecutive Tuesday meetings, each focusing on a central topic (e.g., love, work, death), with interwoven flashbacks, commentary, and personal anecdotes
features: Quotes and lessons distilled from Morrie's teachings

key_concepts_lessons: Facing death helps clarify life’s true priorities.
Love and relationships are more important than material success.
Forgiveness of oneself and others brings peace.
Living authentically and embracing vulnerability enhances fulfillment.
Accepting mortality is crucial for a meaningful life.
The value of mentorship and passing on wisdom.
notable_features: Based on true, deeply emotional conversations
Addresses universal human concerns about life and death
cultural_historical_context: Published in the late 1990s, amidst growing popular interest in memoirs and personal growth literature, the book resonated in an era grappling with questions of fulfillment amid rapid social and technological change. Morrie Schwartz's battle with ALS (Lou Gehrig’s disease) brought further attention to issues surrounding terminal illness, dignity, and end-of-life care.
reception_impact: International bestseller with millions of copies sold
Taught in schools and universities as a modern classic
Inspirational source for discussions on life, death, and values
Adapted into a successful television film and stage play
Praised for emotional impact, accessibility, and humanity; sometimes critiqued for sentimentality
comparable_titles: The Last Lecture by Randy Pausch
Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor E. Frankl
When Breath Becomes Air by Paul Kalanithi
